summaries.example: Imagine two students joining a school club. Treating them equally does not always mean giving them the exact same help. If one student cannot reach the sign-up table, providing a lower table can help both students take part fairly. The important question is: what feature matters in this situation?
summaries.summary: Equality is a way of comparing people or things in one chosen respect. Two people can be equal in one way, such as having the same right to speak, while being different in many other ways. This is not the same as identity, which means being exactly the same thing, or similarity, which means being somewhat alike. In discussions about justice, equality is a complicated idea rather than one simple rule. We must ask what is being compared, which people are included, and what standard should guide the comparison. Formal equality says that relevantly similar cases should be treated alike. Proportional equality says that fair treatment may depend on a person’s relevant situation, contribution, need, or other reason. Moral equality says that all human beings have equal worth and deserve equal concern and respect, not necessarily identical treatment. A presumption of equality starts by favoring equal shares or treatment, while allowing unequal treatment when it can be fairly justified. Philosophers disagree about what justice should equalize: resources, well-being, opportunities, capabilities, or relationships among people. Some think equality is valuable in itself; others think it matters because it reduces suffering, prevents domination, or supports freedom and respect. The entry also considers the view that justice may require giving people enough or helping those who are worst off, even when exact equality is not the goal.
key_ideas: Equality does not mean that everyone is exactly the same. It means being alike in a particular respect.
Whenever we talk about equality, we should ask: equal in what way, and among whom?
Treating everyone exactly alike is not always fair. Needs, responsibilities, or other relevant differences may matter.
Moral equality says that all people have equal worth and deserve respect.
People disagree about whether justice should aim mainly at equal results, equal chances, enough for everyone, or equal social standing.
summaries.why_it_matters: Ideas about equality shape rules at school, in communities, and in government. They help us notice unfair treatment and ask whether differences really matter. Thinking carefully about equality can also prevent a mistake: assuming that fairness always means giving everyone exactly the same thing. It encourages us to consider needs, choices, opportunities, respect, and the effects of social arrangements.

important_terms.definition: A way of comparing people or things to see whether they are the same in one important respect.
The idea that people who are alike in an important way should be treated alike in that way.
The idea that people should receive what is fair for their situation, rather than always receiving the exact same amount.
The idea that every person deserves basic respect and concern, even though people are different.

questions_to_think_about: When is giving everyone the same thing fair?
When might people need different kinds of help to have a fair chance?
What does it mean to respect everyone equally?
Should a person’s choices affect what help they receive?

summaries.example: Suppose a city distributes public transportation funds. An equal-per-person plan might give every neighborhood the same amount. A proportional plan might give more to neighborhoods with greater travel needs or fewer existing options. An opportunity-based plan might focus on whether residents can actually reach work, school, and public services. A relational approach might ask whether some neighborhoods are treated as inferior or excluded from decisions. These are different interpretations of what equality requires, not merely different arithmetic methods.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of equality concerns social and political equality, especially its relation to justice. Equality is not identity: two persons or cases can correspond in one respect while differing in others. Nor is it merely approximate similarity. Any claim that people are equal is incomplete until it specifies the relevant respect, the persons included, and the normative standard governing treatment. Formal equality states that cases equal in a normatively relevant respect should be treated alike. Proportional equality adds that unequal treatment can be just when it tracks relevant differences, such as need, desert, contribution, or disadvantage. Numerical equality—giving everyone the same amount—is therefore only one possible form of proportional equality. Moral equality offers a more fundamental ideal: persons have equal worth and are entitled to equal concern and respect, though this does not imply uniform treatment. The presumption of equality treats equal distribution as the default in political distribution, placing the burden of justification on those who favor unequal shares. The major distributive debate asks what should be equalized, or what currency equality has. Candidates include welfare, resources, opportunities for welfare or advantage, and capabilities to achieve valuable ways of living. These approaches address different problems involving responsibility, luck, differing needs, choice, and the possibility that equal goods produce unequal opportunities. Relational egalitarianism shifts attention from distributions to whether people stand in relations free from domination, stigma, and inferior status. key_ideas: Equality is a three-part comparison: between people or cases, regarding a specified feature, according to a standard of comparison.
Formal equality supplies a structure for justice, but it does not by itself determine which differences are relevant.
Proportional equality explains why equal treatment can sometimes require unequal shares or responses.
Moral equality supports equal dignity and respect, while leaving open which concrete rights, opportunities, or resources people are owed.
The central distributive question is “equality of what?” Competing answers include welfare, resources, opportunities, advantage, and capabilities.
Some theories value equality intrinsically; others value it for its effects, or treat it as part of a broader ideal of justice and equal standing.
summaries.why_it_matters: Equality is central to arguments about law, political participation, economic distribution, and social status. Yet invoking equality does not settle a dispute: it opens further questions about the relevant comparison, the people included, the proper metric, and the reasons that can justify unequal outcomes. These distinctions make it possible to evaluate policies more precisely and to see why people who all appeal to fairness may still disagree.

important_terms.definition: A contested political and moral concept concerning correspondence between persons or cases in a specified respect; it is incomplete until the relevant respect is identified.
The principle that cases equal in a normatively relevant respect should receive equal treatment in that respect.
A principle requiring treatment or distribution to correspond proportionally to relevant differences, such as need, desert, or contribution.
The claim that all persons possess equal moral worth and are owed equal concern and respect, without requiring uniform treatment.
A default rule favoring equal distribution unless relevant differences provide impartial justification for unequal shares.
The dimension or measure in which equality is sought, such as resources, welfare, opportunity, or capabilities.
An approach that evaluates justice by whether people relate as equals, rather than only by comparing distributions.
The view that priority should be given to improving the situation of worse-off people, even if equality itself is not the fundamental value.

questions_to_think_about: Which differences should count as relevant when deciding whether people deserve equal treatment?
Can a society be unequal in resources yet equal in social standing?
Is it fair to hold people responsible for inequalities caused by voluntary choices but not for disadvantages beyond their control?
Should justice prioritize equality, improving the position of the worst off, or ensuring that everyone has enough?
Does equal opportunity require only formally open positions, or also conditions that make opportunities genuinely usable?

summaries.example: A teacher has four students share art supplies. Giving each student one identical box seems equal. But one student is working on a much larger group project, and another has no supplies at home. The class might debate whether fairness means identical boxes, supplies matched to the projects, extra help for the student with fewer resources, or rules that prevent anyone from being left without what they need. Each choice uses a different idea of equality.
summaries.summary: Equality is a relationship of matching in a particular respect. It does not mean that two people are identical in every way. For example, people may have equal legal rights while differing in age, abilities, interests, or resources. Because equality is incomplete without a standard, every equality claim raises questions: Who is being compared? Equal in what? And what rule decides whether a difference matters? The entry describes several principles. Formal equality says that people who are alike in a relevant way should be treated alike. Proportional equality says that fairness may require shares or treatment to reflect relevant differences. Giving everyone the same amount can be fair in some cases, but not in all cases. Moral equality says that people have equal worth and deserve equal concern and respect; it does not require treating everyone identically. The presumption of equality begins with equal distribution as a default and asks those who support unequal distribution to give an impartial justification. Philosophers then debate the “currency” of equality: what should be equalized? Possibilities include material resources, welfare, opportunities, advantages, or capabilities—the real freedoms people have to achieve important ways of living. Some theories focus on responsibility and luck, while relational theories ask whether people are dominated, stigmatized, or treated as socially inferior. Other views argue that justice should prioritize helping the worst off or making sure everyone has enough, rather than pursuing equality as such. Thus, equality is not one complete answer to every justice question; it is a framework for asking what fair comparison and fair treatment require.
key_ideas: Equality always requires a question: equal in what respect?
Formal equality is not enough by itself because it does not tell us which differences matter.
Proportional equality can support different treatment when differences in need, contribution, or responsibility are relevant.
Moral equality means equal human worth, not that everyone has identical talents, choices, or needs.
The presumption of equality makes equal treatment the starting point, but unequal treatment may be justified with reasons that others could accept.
Philosophers disagree about whether justice should equalize resources, welfare, opportunities, capabilities, or social relationships.
summaries.why_it_matters: Many disagreements about fairness are really disagreements about which kind of equality matters. Equal rules may leave people with unequal chances, while equal outcomes may ignore different needs or choices. Learning the distinctions helps students examine school policies, access to opportunities, public resources, and social treatment without assuming that one simple formula solves every problem.

important_terms.definition: A comparison showing that people or cases match in one chosen respect, even though they may differ in other respects.
Treating cases alike when they are alike in a respect that matters for the rule or decision.
Giving people treatment or shares that match relevant differences, rather than automatically giving everyone the same amount.
The principle that all people have equal worth and should receive equal concern and respect.
A starting assumption that equal shares are fair unless a good, impartial reason supports unequal shares.
What a theory says should be made equal, such as money, resources, well-being, chances, or abilities to live well.
A view that justice requires people to relate to one another as social equals, without domination or degrading status differences.

questions_to_think_about: Why might identical treatment produce unfair results?
What makes a difference morally relevant rather than merely noticeable?
Should people receive compensation for disadvantages they did not choose?
Can equal respect support different treatment in different situations?
Would a society be fair if everyone had enough, even if some had much more than others?
